hints: Look closely at the two highest rates, 33 at $40^{\circ}C$ and 32 at $50^{\circ}C$. They are almost the same, and the temperatures tested are $10^{\circ}C$ apart.
Remember the optimum is the temperature with the true maximum rate. With big gaps between readings, can you be sure the peak is exactly on a tested temperature?
walkthrough:
**Spot the trend in the table**

Look at how the rate changes. It rises from 3 to 7 to 16 to 33, stays high at 32, then falls to 14.

This rise then fall shape is classic for temperature and enzyme activity.

**Think about what optimum really means**

The optimum is the temperature where the rate is truly highest.

Because we only measured every $10^{\circ}C$, the real peak could be hiding between two measurements, for example at $42^{\circ}C$ or $47^{\circ}C$.

**Pin down where the peak must be**

The rate is still climbing at $30^{\circ}C$ (16) and has started falling by $60^{\circ}C$ (14).

The high flat top at $40^{\circ}C$ and $50^{\circ}C$ tells us the true maximum lies somewhere between the lower rising point ($30^{\circ}C$) and the upper high point ($50^{\circ}C$).

options.A: $40^{\circ}C$ gave the highest measured rate, but we did not test $41-49^{\circ}C$. The true optimum could be between 40 and 50, so we cannot claim it is exactly 40.
options.B: 32 at $50^{\circ}C$ fits the expected pattern of a peak followed by a fall. It is very close to 33, so it is not an outlier or anomalous result.
options.C: The rate increases up to $40^{\circ}C$ and decreases after $50^{\circ}C$. This shows the true maximum must lie between $30^{\circ}C$ and $50^{\circ}C$.
options.D: At $60^{\circ}C$ the rate is 14, not zero. Some enzyme is still working, so not all enzymes have denatured.
